summary.text: For primes $p\equiv3\pmod4$, reindexing rows and columns by the nonzero quadratic residues expresses the matrix (up to a nonzero scalar) as $U-U^{T}D$, where $U$ is normal and $D$ is a symmetric involution of determinant $1$; an odd-dimensional determinant symmetry then forces singularity. For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, Euler’s criterion and the binomial theorem factor the matrix modulo $p$ into invertible Vandermonde-type factors and a rank-one correction, whose determinant is shown nonzero by Lagrange interpolation together with Wilson’s identity $(((p-1)/2)!)^2=-1$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p=p_n,\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=m!,
\]
where the primes are numbered so that \(p_1=2,p_2=3,\ldots\). For \(n\ge 2\), the prime \(p=p_n\) is odd. The matrix defining \(a(n)\) is
\[
M=\bigl(\chi(i^2-Cj)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m},
\]
where \(\chi(x)=\left(\frac{x}{p}\right)\) is the Legendre symbol. (For prime modulus, the Jacobi symbol appearing in the sequence definition is this Legendre symbol.) We prove
\[
\det M=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]

We use the following linear-algebra lemma.

**Determinant lemma.** Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(W,D\) be square matrices of odd order \(d\), and suppose
\[
WW^T=W^TW,\qquad D^T=D,\qquad D^2=I,\qquad \det D=1.
\]
Then
\[
\det(W-W^TD)=0.
\]

We first prove the lemma when \(W\) is invertible. Put
\[
K=-W^{-1}W^T.
\]
Because \(W\) commutes with \(W^T\), their inverses and all the indicated products commute as well, and hence
\[
K^TK=I.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\det K=(-1)^d\det(W^{-1})\det(W^T)=-1,
\]
since \(d\) is odd. Thus \(\det K\det D=-1\).

We claim that these properties force \(\det(K+D)=0\). Indeed,
\[
K^T+D=K^T(I+KD)
\]
because \(K^TK=I\), while
\[
I+KD=(D+K)D
\]
because \(D^2=I\). Using also \(D^T=D\), invariance of the determinant under transpose, and commutativity of matrix addition, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det(K+D)
 &=\det((K+D)^T)\\
 &=\det(K^T+D)\\
 &=\det(K^T)\det(I+KD)\\
 &=\det K\,\det(D+K)\det D\\
 &=(\det K\det D)\det(K+D)\\
 &=-\det(K+D).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the characteristic is not \(2\), this gives \(\det(K+D)=0\). Finally,
\[
W-W^TD=W(I+KD),
\]
and \(I+KD=(D+K)D\). Therefore the determinant of \(W-W^TD\) contains the zero factor \(\det(D+K)\), proving the invertible case.

For a possibly singular \(W\), introduce an indeterminate \(X\) and work over the polynomial ring \(F[X]\). Set
\[
\widetilde W=W+XI,
\]
regarding the entries of \(W\) as constant polynomials. The matrix \(\widetilde W\) is still normal with respect to transpose:
\[
\widetilde W\widetilde W^T=\widetilde W^T\widetilde W,
\]
because the extra scalar matrix \(XI\) commutes with everything and \(WW^T=W^TW\). Also,
\[
\det\widetilde W=\det(XI+W)

a monic polynomial of degree \(d\), so it is not the zero polynomial. Thus \(\widetilde W\) is invertible over the fraction field \(F(X)\). The already proved invertible case, applied over \(F(X)\), gives
\[
\det(\widetilde W-\widetilde W^TD)=0.
\]
The inclusion \(F[X]\hookrightarrow F(X)\) is injective, so this determinant is already the zero polynomial in \(F[X]\). Evaluating at \(X=0\) gives \(\det(W-W^TD)=0\), proving the determinant lemma.

We now turn to the number-theoretic matrix.

## 1. Vanishing when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

Assume \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(m=(p-1)/2\) is odd. Work in the field \(\mathbb F_p\), and continue to write \(\chi\) for its quadratic character, with \(\chi(0)=0\). We use the standard properties
\[
\chi(xy)=\chi(x)\chi(y),\qquad \chi(x)\in\{1,-1\}\quad(x\ne0),
\]
and
\[
\chi(-1)=-1
\]
because \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Let \(G\) be the multiplicative subgroup of nonzero squares in \(\mathbb F_p^\times\). It has \(m\) elements.

The map
\[
\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\longrightarrow G,\qquad i\longmapsto i^2
\]
is a bijection. Indeed, equality \(i^2=i'^2\) modulo \(p\) implies \(i\equiv i'\) or \(i\equiv-i'\pmod p\). The second alternative is impossible for two integers between \(1\) and \(m\), because then \(i+i'<p\). Thus the map is injective, and both sets have \(m\) elements.

For every \(x\in\mathbb F_p^\times\), define its square representative by
\[
\operatorname{sqrep}(x)=\chi(x)x.
\]
Because \(\chi(-1)=-1\), precisely one of \(x,-x\) is a square, and \(\operatorname{sqrep}(x)\) is that square. Multiplication by the nonzero element \(C=m!\) permutes the pairs \(\{x,-x\}\). Since \(1,\ldots,m\) give exactly one representative of every such pair, the map
\[
\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\longrightarrow G,\qquad
j\longmapsto \operatorname{sqrep}(Cj)
\]
is also a bijection. Here \(C\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), since every factor of \(m!\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(p\).

For each \(q\in G\), let \(w(q)\) be the unique element \(Cj\) whose square representative is \(q\), and put
\[
\eta(q)=\chi(w(q))\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
By the definition of square representative,
\[
q=\eta(q)w(q),
\qquad	ext{and hence also}\qquad
w(q)=\eta(q)q.
\]

Define a rational matrix \(U\), with rows and columns indexed by \(G\), by
\[
U_{r,q}=\chi(r-q)+\chi(r+q).
\]
We first show that \(U\) is normal with respect to transpose:
\[
UU^T=U^TU.
\]
For fixed \(r,r'\in G\), reindex a sum over \(q\in G\) by the bijection
\[
q\longmapsto rr'q^{-1}.
\]
Every element of \(G\) is a square, so multiplying an argument of \(\chi\) by an element of \(G\) does not change its quadratic character. Consequently,
\[
U_{r,\,rr'q^{-1}}=U_{q,r'},
\qquad
U_{r',\,rr'q^{-1}}=U_{q,r}.
\]
For example,
\[
r-rr'q^{-1}=rq^{-1}(q-r'),\qquad
r+rr'q^{-1}=rq^{-1}(q+r'),
\]
and \(rq^{-1}\in G\), which proves the first identity; the second is analogous. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(UU^T)_{r,r'}
 &=\sum_{q\in G}U_{r,q}U_{r',q}\\
 &=\sum_{q\in G}U_{q,r'}U_{q,r}\\
 &=(U^TU)_{r,r'}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now define the diagonal matrix
\[
D=\operatorname{diag}(\eta(q))_{q\in G}.
\]
Clearly \(D^T=D\) and \(D^2=I\). We also need its determinant. Reindexing its diagonal product by the column bijection above gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det D
 &=\prod_{q\in G}\eta(q)
 =\prod_{j=1}^m\chi(Cj)\\
 &=\chi\left(\prod_{j=1}^m Cj\right)
 =\chi(C^m m!)
 =\chi(C^{m+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(C\ne0\), \(\chi(C)=\pm1\), and since \(m\) is odd, \(m+1\) is even. Hence
\[
\det D=\chi(C)^{m+1}=1.
\]

Define another rational matrix, again indexed by \(G\), by
\[
N_{r,q}=\chi(r-w(q)).
\]
We relate it to \(U\) and \(D\). Write
\[
A_{r,q}=\chi(r-q),\qquad B_{r,q}=\chi(r+q),
\]
so that \(U=A+B\). Since \(\chi(-x)=-\chi(x)\) for all \(x\) when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\),
\[
(A-B)_{r,q}=-U^T_{r,q}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
-U^T_{r,q}=-\chi(q-r)-\chi(q+r)
=\chi(r-q)-\chi(r+q).
\]
For a fixed column \(q\), there are two cases. If \(\eta(q)=1\), then \(w(q)=q\), and
\[
(U-U^TD)_{r,q}=(A+B)_{r,q}+(A-B)_{r,q}=2\chi(r-q)=2N_{r,q}.
\]
If \(\eta(q)=-1\), then \(w(q)=-q\), and
\[
(U-U^TD)_{r,q}=(A+B)_{r,q}-(A-B)_{r,q}=2\chi(r+q)=2N_{r,q}.
\]
Thus, in all cases,
\[
2N=U-U^TD.
\]

The matrix \(U\) has odd order \(|G|=m\), is normal, and \(D\) is symmetric, satisfies \(D^2=I\), and has determinant \(1\). The determinant lemma over \(\mathbb Q\) therefore yields
\[
\det(U-U^TD)=0.
\]
Since \(U-U^TD=2N\) and \(2\ne0\) in \(\mathbb Q\), it follows that
\[
\det N=0.
\]

Finally, reindex the rows of \(N\) by \(r=i^2\) and its columns by \(q=\operatorname{sqrep}(Cj)\). Under these bijections, \(w(q)=Cj\), so the reindexed entry is
\[
N_{i^2,\operatorname{sqrep}(Cj)}=\chi(i^2-Cj),
\]
exactly the corresponding entry of \(M\). Independent row and column permutations can only multiply a determinant by signs, and therefore preserve whether it is zero. Hence \(\det M=0\). This proves the implication
\[
p\equiv3\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)=0.
\]

## 2. Nonvanishing when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)

Assume now that \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Then \(p\ge5\) and
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2}
\]
is even. We prove that \(\det M\ne0\) by showing that its reduction modulo \(p\) has nonzero determinant.

In \(\mathbb F_p\), put
\[
a_i=i,\qquad x_i=a_i^2=i^2,
\qquad t_j=-C a_j=-Cj
\quad(1\le i,j\le m).
\]
The elements \(a_i\) are nonzero and distinct. The elements \(x_i\) are also distinct: if \(a_i^2=a_{i'}^2\), then \(a_i=a_{i'}\) or \(a_i=-a_{i'}\); the latter is impossible because \(1\le i+i'\le2m=p-1\), so it cannot be divisible by \(p\). Likewise, the \(t_j\) are nonzero and distinct because \(C\ne0\).

Euler’s criterion says that, viewed as an element of \(\mathbb F_p\),
\[
\chi(y)=y^{(p-1)/2}=y^m
\]
for every \(y\in\mathbb F_p\), including \(y=0\). Therefore the reduction modulo \(p\) of \(M\) is the matrix
\[
\overline M_{i,j}=(x_i+t_j)^m.
\]
It remains to prove \(\det\overline M\ne0\).

Let \(V\) be the \(m\times m\) Vandermonde matrix
\[
V_{i,k}=x_i^k\qquad(0\le k\le m-1),
\]
and let
\[
W_{k,j}=\binom mk t_j^{m-k}
\qquad(0\le k\le m-1,\ 1\le j\le m).
\]
Since \(2m=p-1\), Fermat’s theorem gives
\[
x_i^m=(a_i^2)^m=a_i^{p-1}=1.
\]
Expanding \((x_i+t_j)^m\) and separating the term with exponent \(k=m\), we get
\[
\overline M=VW+J,
\]
where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix.

Both \(V\) and \(W\) are invertible. The Vandermonde determinant of \(V\) is
\[
\det V=\prod_{i<i'}(x_{i'}-x_i),
\]
which is nonzero because the \(x_i\) are distinct. To see that \(W\) is invertible, factor it as follows: first take a Vandermonde matrix in the distinct elements \(t_j\), transpose it, reverse the order of its rows so that the powers become \(m-1-k\), multiply on the right by \(\operatorname{diag}(t_j)\), and multiply on the left by
\[
\operatorname{diag}\left(\binom m0,\binom m1,\ldots,\binom m{m-1}\right).
\]
This gives exactly \(W\), since \(t_j^{m-1-k}t_j=t_j^{m-k}\). The reversed transposed Vandermonde factor is invertible because the \(t_j\) are distinct, and \(\operatorname{diag}(t_j)\) is invertible because every \(t_j\ne0\). Finally, each \(\binom mk\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). Indeed,
\[
\binom mk k!(m-k)!=m!,
\]
and the right side is nonzero modulo \(p\); hence none of the three factors on the left can vanish. Thus \(W\) is invertible.

We next convert the all-ones correction \(J\) into a rank-one determinant factor. For each \(j\), define
\[
P_j=\prod_{\ell\ne j}(t_j-t_\ell),
\qquad
z_j=(t_jP_j)^{-1}.
\]
All these inverses exist because the \(t_j\) are nonzero and pairwise distinct.

We use the elementary Lagrange-interpolation identity
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{f(t_j)}{P_j}
=[X^{m-1}]f(X)
\tag{1}
\]
for every polynomial \(f\) of degree less than \(m\). To justify it, write the Lagrange interpolation formula
\[
f(X)=\sum_{j=1}^m f(t_j)
\frac{\prod_{\ell\ne j}(X-t_\ell)}
     {\prod_{\ell\ne j}(t_j-t_\ell)}.
\]
The coefficient of \(X^{m-1}\) in the \(j\)-th basis polynomial is \(1/P_j\), which gives (1).

Apply (1) to \(f(X)=X^d\), for \(0\le d<m\). It gives
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{t_j^d}{P_j}
=\begin{cases}
1,&d=m-1,\\
0,&d\ne m-1.
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
\]
Using the definition of \(W\) and \(z\), for \(0\le k<m\) we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
(Wz)_k
 &=\sum_j \binom mk t_j^{m-k}(t_jP_j)^{-1}\\
 &=\binom mk\sum_j\frac{t_j^{m-1-k}}{P_j}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (2), this equals \(1\) for \(k=0\) and \(0\) for \(k>0\). Thus \(Wz=e_0\), the first coordinate vector. The first column of \(V\) consists entirely of ones, so
\[
VWz=Ve_0=\mathbf 1,
\]
where \(\mathbf1\) is the all-ones column vector.

Let
\[
B=I+z\mathbf1^T.
\]
Then
\[
(VW)B=VW+(VWz)\mathbf1^T=VW+\mathbf1\mathbf1^T=VW+J=\overline M.
\]
The standard rank-one determinant formula gives
\[
\det B=1+\mathbf1^Tz=1+\sum_{j=1}^m z_j.
\]
For completeness, this formula follows by multilinearity of the determinant: in expanding the columns of \(I+z\mathbf1^T\), any term choosing the rank-one contribution in two different columns has two proportional columns and vanishes; the term choosing none is \(1\), and the terms choosing it in exactly one column sum to \(\mathbf1^Tz\).

It remains to prove
\[
1+\sum_jz_j\ne0.
\tag{3}
\]
Introduce
\[
Q(X)=\prod_{j=1}^m(X-t_j).
\]
This is monic of degree \(m\). Since \(Q(X)-Q(0)\) is divisible by \(X\), define a polynomial \(g\) by
\[
Q(X)=Q(0)+Xg(X).
\]
Then \(g\) has degree \(m-1\) and leading coefficient \(1\). At a root \(t_j\) of \(Q\),
\[
g(t_j)=-Q(0)t_j^{-1}.
\]
Applying (1) to \(g\), whose coefficient of \(X^{m-1}\) is \(1\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
 &=\sum_j\frac{g(t_j)}{P_j}
 =-Q(0)\sum_j\frac1{t_jP_j}
 =-Q(0)\sum_jz_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
Q(0)\sum_jz_j=-1.
\tag{4}
\]
We can evaluate \(Q(0)\) explicitly. Since \(t_j=-Cj\),
\[
Q(0)=\prod_j(-t_j)=\prod_j(Cj)=C^m m!=C^{m+1}.
\tag{5}
\]

We now use Wilson’s theorem to determine \(C^2\). Splitting the product \((p-1)!\) into its lower and upper halves, and pairing every upper-half element with its negative in the lower half, gives
\[
(p-1)!=C\cdot((-1)^mC)=(-1)^mC^2
\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_p.
\]
Wilson’s theorem says \((p-1)!=-1\). Since \(m\) is even, \((-1)^m=1\), and therefore
\[
C^2=-1.
\tag{6}
\]

Suppose, contrary to (3), that \(1+\sum_jz_j=0\). Then \(\sum_jz_j=-1\), so (4) gives \(Q(0)=1\). By (5), this says
\[
C^{m+1}=1.
\]
Using (6),
\[
(-1)^{m+1}=(C^2)^{m+1}=(C^{m+1})^2=1.
\]
But \(m\) is even, so \(m+1\) is odd and the left side is \(-1\). This would imply \(-1=1\) in \(\mathbb F_p\), impossible because \(p\) is odd. Thus (3) holds.

We have now shown that every factor in
\[
\det\overline M=\det V\,\det W\left(1+\sum_jz_j\right)
\]
is nonzero. Therefore \(\det\overline M\ne0\) in \(\mathbb F_p\). If the original integer determinant \(\det M\) were zero, its reduction modulo \(p\) would also be zero, a contradiction. Hence
\[
p\equiv1\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(n)=\det M\ne0.
\]

Finally, for \(n\ge2\), \(p_n>2\), so \(p_n\) is odd and its residue modulo \(4\) is either \(1\) or \(3\). The first part proves vanishing in the residue class \(3\), and the second proves nonvanishing in the residue class \(1\). Consequently,
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }
\]
for every \(n\ge2\), as required.
